title: Hiking Time Calculator: Naismith Estimates
description: Estimate hiking time from distance and ascent with the Hiking Time Calculator — a simple Naismith-style rule, transparently applied. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 12 miles with 3,000 ft of climbing prices at about 5 hours 30 minutes by the rule — before rests, photos and the pub at the end.
quick_answer: The Hiking Time Calculator estimates how long a hike takes from its distance and total ascent, using a Naismith-style rule: a base pace over the ground plus an allowance for height gained. Enter the route's two numbers and read the time your daylight, water and group decisions should hang from.

body.t: Start time + Naismith total + margin versus sunset: the oldest safety equation in hill walking, computed in seconds.
The longer-but-flatter route versus the shorter climb: both priced in time, the trade becomes a choice instead of a discovery at the steep part.

A guidebook's distance and ascent become your time estimate before you commit — the trailhead sign's two numbers are all this needs.
12 mi at 3 mph = 4 h; 3,000 ft at 30 min/1,000 ft = 1 h 30 min; total ≈ 5 h 30 min. Add an hour of living — food, views, boots off — and the day is 6½ hours, planned.
5 miles with 400 ft of climb: 1 h 40 min + 12 min ≈ 1 h 52 min. The rule stays proportionate at ramble scale, which is why it has survived a century of use.

faq: Does this replace a specialist tool or professional measurement?
No. It is a century-old planning rule applied transparently. Mountain judgement — weather, terrain, the party's strength — remains yours and your leader's.
Is my input uploaded?
No. Distance and ascent are computed with in your browser.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Nothing about a trail is traffic; conditions are the walker's to read on the day.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Trails wind more. Enter the trail distance — from a route plan or a guidebook — not the crow's figure.
Can route results change over time?
Your fitness changes the input pace, and paths change their lengths. Recalculate per season and per route.
What pace does the rule assume?
About 3 mph (5 km/h) on the flat, plus the climb allowance. Slower parties should scale the base pace — the calculator's structure accepts the honesty.
Should I add time for descent?
Steep descents cost real parties real time. The classic rule ignores them; prudent planners add a margin on very steep ground.
How long for a walk with 600 m of climb over 14 km?
Flat time 14 ÷ 5 = 2 h 48 min; climb 600 m ≈ 30 min per 300 m → 1 h; total ≈ 3 h 48 min, rests excluded.
Does the rule work for running?
Trail runners move faster than Naismith's walking assumption — scale the base pace to your running pace and keep the climb allowance as a starting guess.
Snow and ice conditions?
The rule assumes walkable ground. Winter conditions multiply times in ways only experience calibrates; this estimate is the summer truth.
